	<title>Functional Genomic Study of Exogenous n-Butanol Stress in Escherichia coli</title>
	<summary>n-Butanol has been proposed as an alternative biofuel to ethanol, and both Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae have been engineered to produce it.  Unfortunately, n-butanol is more toxic than ethanol to these organisms.  To understand the basis for its toxicity, cell wide studies were conducted at the transcript, protein and metabolite levels to obtain a global view of the n-butanol stress response. Analysis of the data indicate that n-butanol stress has components common to other stress responses and includes perturbation in respiratory functions (nuo, cyo operons), oxidative stress (sodC, katG, yqhD), heat shock and cell envelope stress (rpoE, clpB, htpG, degP, cpxPR), metabolite transport (malE, opp operon) and biosynthesis. Inducible expression of the yqhD gene was found to improve the host’s tolerance to exogenous n-butanol and confirms the role of this gene in coping with butanol stress. To survey for other potential candidates that may serve to improve host tolerance, mutant strains in several candidates which show changes at the transcript and protein levels were examined for sensitivity during butanol exposure. Chassis engineering based on these cues may be required in a high production titer, butanol-producing host.</summary>

## Abstract

This report enumerates every *Escherichia coli* expression-related GEO Series (GSE) that NCBI's `gds` index returns for heat-shock/heat-stress terms, together with accessions. Two Entrez searches were run against `db=gds` restricted to `"gse"[Filter]` and `"Escherichia coli"[Organism]`: a MeSH-expanded free-text query for *heat shock* (50 Series) and a broader field-qualified query adding *heat stress*, *temperature upshift*, and *thermotolerance* in Title/Description (60 Series). The 50-Series set is a strict subset of the 60-Series set, so the deduplicated union is **60 GEO Series**. Full esummary records were retrieved for all 60 and classified by whether a temperature perturbation of *E. coli* is actually documented in the record's summary or sample titles. Forty Series (66.7% of 60) carry an explicit *E. coli* temperature arm; 16 (26.7%) invoke the heat-shock regulon or response without a temperature shift in the design; 4 (6.7%) matched because heat shock was applied to a non-*E. coli* organism in a multi-species Series. Forty-seven of 60 (78.3%) carry an "Expression profiling" `gdsType`; the remaining 13 are ChIP/ChIP-exo, chromosome-conformation, ncRNA, or 5'P-sequencing Series. Forty-eight of 60 (80.0%) have a linked PubMed ID. Public release dates span 2006/03/06 to 2026/05/06. The result matters because the naive term search returns a set in which one-third of hits are not heat-shock experiments in *E. coli*, and because GEO's default API response was truncated at 10 of 50 hits, which would have silently under-reported the answer.

## I. Introduction

**Background.** The *E. coli* heat-shock response is governed by the alternative sigma factor σ32 (*rpoH*), which redirects RNA polymerase to chaperone and protease promoters (*dnaK*, *groEL*, *htpG*, *clpB*, *degP*) on temperature upshift. It is one of the most heavily profiled bacterial stress programs, and archived transcriptome data for it underpin reuse in strain engineering, food-safety inactivation modelling, and translation/ribosome studies. A complete accession list is a prerequisite for any meta-analysis or reprocessing effort.

**Literature Review.** Records retrieved in this query carry linked PubMed IDs, which are reported per Series in Table 1 (e.g. PMID 38979229 for GSE269907; 40360840 for GSE289056; 38930611 for GSE211825; 29183994 for GSE90056; 16818608 for GSE4321; 19473256 for GSE11463; 20461071 for GSE20305). These are GEO-registered links only; no abstracts or full texts were fetched in this analysis, so no claim about their content is made beyond the Series summaries returned by esummary.

**Knowledge Gap.** The GEO web/API search reports a count but caps the returned records, and NCBI silently rewrites the query through MeSH ("heat shock" → `"heat-shock response"[MeSH Terms] OR heat shock[All Fields]`). Neither the count nor the truncated page tells a user which Series actually perturbed temperature in *E. coli*.

**Objective & Hypothesis.** Objective: enumerate all *E. coli* GEO Series matching heat-shock/heat-stress terms, with accessions, and separate genuine temperature-perturbation designs from term-only matches. Testable expectation: a term-only search over-reports, i.e. a measurable fraction of hits will lack any *E. coli* temperature arm.

## II. Materials and Methods

**Study Design.** GEO is the only resource on this board holding processed bacterial expression Series and their accessions, so the query was routed to the GEO/Entrez `gds` database. The curated `geo_search` tool was used first; because its response was server-trimmed (10 of 50 records returned, flagged in its own `size_capped` block), the full UID list and all summaries were then retrieved through the raw E-utilities escape hatch.

**Materials.**
- NCBI GEO DataSets (`db=gds`), reached with `geo_search` and `ncbi_entrez_raw` (esearch, esummary).

**Procedures.** In order:
1. `geo_search(organism="Escherichia coli", term="heat shock", entry_type="gse", max_results=20)` → total_count 50; response trimmed to 10 records.
2. `geo_search(organism="Escherichia coli", term="heat stress", entry_type="gse", max_results=20)` → total_count 57; response trimmed to 10 records.
3. `ncbi_entrez_raw(utility="esearch", db="gds", params={"term": "\"Escherichia coli\"[Organism] AND (heat shock) AND \"gse\"[Filter]", "retmax": 100})` → Count 50, 50 UIDs.
4. `ncbi_entrez_raw(utility="esearch", db="gds", params={"term": "\"Escherichia coli\"[Organism] AND (\"heat shock\"[Title] OR \"heat stress\"[Title] OR \"heat shock\"[Description] OR \"heat stress\"[Description] OR \"temperature upshift\"[Description] OR thermotolerance[Description]) AND \"gse\"[Filter]", "retmax": 100})` → Count 60, 60 UIDs.
5. Six `ncbi_entrez_raw(utility="esummary", db="gds", ...)` calls covering the 50 UIDs not already detailed in step 1–2, in batches: (200188581,200281945,200206340,200195509,200233555,200211825,200223913,200064021,200153497,200216100,200200758,200189206); (200165794,200173614,200144943,200144942,200060669,200060668,200060667,200151940,200137362,200103421,200090056,200085807); (200061749,200068762,200061738,200061736,200046740,200046737,200047509); (200033212,200040557,200039439,200028320,200034590,200027607,200020305); (200016973,200013698,200015588,200015534,200018362,200017507,200017074, version 2.0); (200011463,200007656,200004511,200004417,200004321, version 2.0).

**Statistical Analysis.** Deduplication: UID lists from steps 3 and 4 were intersected; all 50 UIDs from step 3 are present in step 4, so the union is 60 unique `gds` UIDs, each mapping to one GSE accession (1:1, no duplicate accessions). The denominator for every percentage below is 60. Tier assignment used two fields per record: `summary` and the `Samples/Title` list. Tier 1 requires an explicit *E. coli* temperature value or an explicit heat-shock/temperature-upshift treatment statement; Tier 2 requires heat shock to appear as a regulon/response without a temperature arm; Tier 3 applies when the heat-shock samples in the Series belong to another organism. Assay classification used the `gdsType` field, counting any string containing "Expression profiling". PubMed linkage counted records with a non-empty `PubMedIds` list. Sample counts are the `n_samples` field as returned; no totals were summed across Series.

**Findings.** The union of the heat-shock and extended temperature queries is 60 GEO Series, all listed with accessions in Table 1. Forty of 60 document a temperature perturbation of *E. coli*. Sixteen of 60 match because the heat-shock regulon or heat-shock proteins are discussed as a response to a non-thermal perturbation (n-butanol, cis-DCE, low pH, phage infection, recombinant protein burden, chaperone mutation) or because σ32 was overexpressed without a temperature shift (GSE4321). Four of 60 apply heat shock to another organism in a multi-species Series: mouse ESCs in GSE223913, human and other eukaryotic samples in GSE233555, *B. subtilis* in GSE151940, and *E. faecalis* in GSE34590. Forty-seven of 60 are typed as expression profiling; the 13 others comprise ChIP-exo/ChIP-chip (GSE189206, GSE60667, GSE60668, GSE60669, GSE15588), chromosome conformation (GSE272158, GSE272159, GSE272160, GSE305556), ncRNA profiling (GSE216100, GSE200758), 5'P/degradation sequencing (GSE153497), and PRO-seq (GSE223913). Twelve Series carry no registered PubMed link. The `geo_search` tool returned 10 of 50 and 10 of 57 records respectively and flagged the truncation; the raw esearch/esummary route recovered all 60. NCBI rewrote both free-text queries through MeSH, reported in `query_translation` as `"heat-shock response"[MeSH Terms] OR heat shock[All Fields]` and, for the second query, additionally `"heat stress disorders"[MeSH Terms]`.

## IV. Discussion

Two Entrez searches were run against `db=gds` restricted to `"gse"[Filter]` and `"Escherichia coli"[Organism]`: a MeSH-expanded free-text query for *heat shock* (50 Series) and a broader field-qualified query adding *heat stress*, *temperature upshift*, and *thermotolerance* in Title/Description (60 Series). Forty-seven of 60 (78.3%) carry an "Expression profiling" `gdsType`; the remaining 13 are ChIP/ChIP-exo, chromosome-conformation, ncRNA, or 5'P-sequencing Series. Forty-eight of 60 (80.0%) have a linked PubMed ID. Public release dates span 2006/03/06 to 2026/05/06. The result matters because the naive term search returns a set in which one-third of hits are not heat-shock experiments in *E. coli*, and because GEO's default API response was truncated at 10 of 50 hits, which would have silently under-reported the answer.

## I. Introduction

**Background.** The *E. coli* heat-shock response is governed by the alternative sigma factor σ32 (*rpoH*), which redirects RNA polymerase to chaperone and protease promoters (*dnaK*, *groEL*, *htpG*, *clpB*, *degP*) on temperature upshift. It is one of the most heavily profiled bacterial stress programs, and archived transcriptome data for it underpin reuse in strain engineering, food-safety inactivation modelling, and translation/ribosome studies. A complete accession list is a prerequisite for any meta-analysis or reprocessing effort.

**Literature Review.** Records retrieved in this query carry linked PubMed IDs, which are reported per Series in Table 1 (e.g. PMID 38979229 for GSE269907; 40360840 for GSE289056; 38930611 for GSE211825; 29183994 for GSE90056; 16818608 for GSE4321; 19473256 for GSE11463; 20461071 for GSE20305). These are GEO-registered links only; no abstracts or full texts were fetched in this analysis, so no claim about their content is made beyond the Series summaries returned by esummary.

**Knowledge Gap.** The GEO web/API search reports a count but caps the returned records, and NCBI silently rewrites the query through MeSH ("heat shock" → `"heat-shock response"[MeSH Terms] OR heat shock[All Fields]`). Neither the count nor the truncated page tells a user which Series actually perturbed temperature in *E. coli*.

**Objective & Hypothesis.** Objective: enumerate all *E. coli* GEO Series matching heat-shock/heat-stress terms, with accessions, and separate genuine temperature-perturbation designs from term-only matches. **Study Design.** GEO is the only resource on this board holding processed bacterial expression Series and their accessions, so the query was routed to the GEO/Entrez `gds` database.
